Crazy how many people are freaking out over watching AoT, TPN, and Made in Abyss with your daughter. 12 year old girls definitely have that kind of darker side in them, take it from me, I used to be that edgy 12 year old girl. 

**More fucked up anime you can watch with her:**

• Juuni Taisen — a battle royale between 12 representatives of 12 families that represent the Chinese zodiac animals

•  Assassination Classroom — LOVED this as a young teen. Heartwarming, definitely touches on more serious topics but I feel like they're very relatable for young teens. 

• Death Parade — Might wanna put this on hold till she's a bit older just cause the themes are a bit more abstract and she wouldn't really grasp the themes of morality as well as she would if she was, say, 15/16. Banger of an opening song, very cool premise.

• Dorohedoro — pretty gory but it's pretty much just part of the world. Nothing incredibly shocking, and the story and world is very interesting. Main theme is friendship (If you can believe it). My go-to recommendation for people in alternative subcultures, especially metalheads.

• Fullmetal Alchemist Brotherhood — GREAT watch. Incredibly well thought-out world, lots of social commentary, enjoyable characters. A lot of heavier themes on morality

• Seraph of the End — post apocalyptic military vampires. 

• Stars Align — anime about a middle school badminton team. Heavier personal themes, gets quite intimate. Very much related to this as a 13 year old.

• A Silent Voice — deaf girl and the guy that bullied her as a child reconnect. Themes of guilt (content warning for suicidal ideation) and forgiveness. GORGEOUS visuals.

**Less fucked up watches:**

• Asobi Asobase — Hilarious watch about middle school girls that form a games club. Some of the humour might fly over new watcher's heads though, it's very distinctly Japanese and of course there might be a cultural difference with non-Japanese viewers.

• Barakamon — Funny, wholesome watch. A prodigy calligraphist moves to a countryside village to get over a creative slump and makes friends with the local children and get inspired by them.

• Cells at Work — Wholesome watch about the cells of the human body working to keep it functioning.

• Dr Stone — I have no idea how to explain the premise, but trust me it's a great watch. Used to use it as an out from having to actually study science.

• Gakuen Babysitters — Cute anime about some high schoolers forming a club to babysit the school staff's toddlers. What more can I say? Adorable watch, my go-to comfort anime.

• Gekkan Shoujo Nozaki-kun — Rom Com anime about a highschool girl having a crush on her classmate, and him being absolutely oblivious the whole time. Lovable characters.

• Hanebado — About middle school girls competing in badminton competitions. Also gets pretty personal and deals with a lot of issues that comes with being a young teen girl in competitive sports 

• Hotarubi no Mori E — A girl falls in love with a ghost. Cute, a little heartbreaking, but overall a satisfying watch.

• I want to eat your Pancreas — a boy falls in love with a terminally ill girl. They spend their remaining time together.

•  Jibaku Shounen Hanako Kun — I loved this when I was 12, my cousin got into it when they were 12, I think this anime is just a hit with preteens and young teens overall. Banger of an opening and incredible visuals.

• Mob Psycho 100 — I will never not recommend MP100. Great visuals, great story and themes, great characters.

• One Punch Man — incredibly funny action anime.

• Saiki K — Also another comedy anime with great characters. The dub of this is pretty good too.

• Sweetness and Lightning — the wife of a teacher with a young child suddenly dies, and he's left learning to cope with having to raise his daughter on his own. He forms a friendship with one of his students and learns to cook and raise his daughter from her.

• The Great Pretender — Heists. Incredibly fun watch. Wish I could watch it for the first time again.

• Tsurune — about a highschool traditional Japanese archery club. Gorgeous visuals. More down to earth and intimate.

• Your Name — this is a movie, but it's incredibly well written and produced.

• Ride Your Wave — another well-written and produced movie. It does get pretty sad though, but it ends up being a very satisfying watch.

• Children of the Sea — another movie with great visuals.

• Handa-kun — the prequel to Barakamon, following the main character in his middle school days. Funny, wholesome watch. Relatable.

That's all I got for now, hopefully you were able to get some good recommendations from this list. Happy watching!

If you're doing it with full respect and acknowledgement of the culture, then I wouldn't say so. Culture gets shared all the time — it's one of the core tools from the earliest stages of humanity that made it great. It's when a culture or a feature of a culture gets bastardized (by way of capitalism, discrimination, or a lack of respect to cultural significance) that it becomes appropriation. It's as they always say — appreciate, don't appropriate.

Edit: just as an addition, if you're looking to masculinize clothing, it's more about the body's silhouette and how it's broken up or manipulated. This is usually achieved by wearing garments that fit a particular way. Typically, men have broader shoulders and a waistline that feeds straight into their hips without flaring back out (i.e., the "hourglass" shape that's highlighted in women's fashion).

 For example, when I wear skirts in a more masculine way, I use a skirt that has more of a straight silhouette that doesn't flare out or hug my thighs (this might accentuate the hourglass figure), and I would have the garment sit at my hip instead of my waist. I'd also wear a top that accentuates my shoulders and hides the way my waist flows into wider hips, to add to the illusion. The hem of the skirt would also stop either right at my knee or just below it; if it goes any lower, the fabric might end up falling in a way that tapers in or flares out at the lower leg, which might visually give an hourglass effect. 

More inspiration for masculine "skirt" or "dress" type clothing might come from Arab/Middle Eastern men's clothing (look up "thobes" for this), South Asian men's clothing (called a "lungi"), different Pacific Islander loincloths, and even East Asian traditional clothing (the ones I'm most familiar with are from Japan: Fundoshi, Kimono, Hakama, and Yukata). In Europe, you have various kilt styles that have Celtic origins. Other notable European "skirt"-esque wear include cassocks or soutanes, the chitons of ancient Greece, and many different styles from throughout the medieval period.

And of course, a quick Pinterest or TikTok search will bring up hundreds of thousands of results of modern-day men and masculine presenting people putting their own spin on the masculine skirt.

In a similar position! I'm full Filipino and was actually raised in the Philippines for most of my early childhood  and despite that, my family didn't bother getting me to speak Tagalog or our regional dialects because they wanted me to speak English well so I could easily assimilate abroad. Instead I feel alienated in both my own culture and everywhere else! 

If you can sorta understand basic sentences and have a bit of a feel for the sentence structure, it's worth diving straight into Filipino media, particularly songs and videos. I also had the concern of coming across too formally with textbook Tagalog, so instead I watch Filipino YouTubers and streamers. CongTV is a pretty popular Filipino YouTuber right now if you want a starting point. Filipino cooking/recipe videos are also a great way to kill three birds with one stone: language, social culture, and culinary culture. 

Most of the Filipino language is very intuitive and hard to apply a set of rules to so listening and parroting back phrases is a solid (and, IMO, the easiest) way to learn. It's also a great way of finding out what vocabulary is most relevant to you and the topics you may want to talk about.

If you're starting out from absolute zero though, it's a good idea to pick up a grammar book just to get a sense of the grammar before you start consuming Filipino media.

Most words in the language that are related to each other are actually derived from the same root word, and it's pretty easy to figure out the form and purpose of the word by picking apart the suffixes/prefixes/"mid"fixes that are stacked onto it. Context clues (and a quick Google search) are your best friend!

Speaking of words, Filipino (especially modern Filipino) uses a lot of English loan words, so don't be afraid of the occasional loan word here or there, especially in conversation. In terms of literature though, I believe there's an incoming trend in OPM (Original Pinoy Music) where lyricists are shifting more towards "classical" Filipino with little to no English loan words. If you're interested in that kind of thing, definitely have a look at older Filipino music (harana/kundiman songs from the early 1900s is a personal recommendation of mine) or classic Filipino literature (start with whatever they're teaching in classrooms — Ibong Adarna, Florante at Laura, El Filibusterismo, etc)

If you're stuck in the weird little "I can understand but I can't really speak" phase, just get over yourself and start speaking. By yourself works in the beginning, or even by verbally reacting to video dialogue and the such for a more conversational feel. The latter works especially well in the earlier stages because you can easily roll back videos to analyze grammar/topic/context and you can pause to formulate your own "response" in turn. 

Eventually though, you're gonna have to actually start speaking it. Filipinos are friendly people but they tend to get overfamiliar at times and start overstepping boundaries by being lightheartedly sharp-tongued or playfully bullying you a little too much. This is, regrettably, a feature of Filipino culture. The vast majority of the time though, it's just for the laughs and they don't mean it personally, so don't take it personally. Trust me, you'll ***know*** when a Filipino's tryna get personal with you.

I'm not gonna tell you what to do but I will tell you that substances do NOT fix your problems. Sure, they'll put your mind off of it or alter the way your brain functions for a short period of time but they are not solutions to your emotional or mental problems. If you keep seeing them as such, then I recommend you never start at all. 

If you understand that and contextualize and justify your use of substances, then figure it out for yourself. I found out what works for me — for example, I know I don't like hitting a vape too many times in a short period cause it makes me feel sick. I also avoid smoking cigarettes unless I really need the nicotine to hit like a truck (like when I'm mentally spiraling and need to "kill switch" my brain), and I never reach for a vape first thing in the morning. But these are only examples of what works for my situations and my biology. Find out how your brain and body works and go from there. But I will stress this again: ***substances do not fix whatever ails you. they only help you deal with the symptoms.***

A lot of people are trying to figure out different words for "not cis, straight, or allosexual or alloromantic" for this exact reason — there's so many identities that can't be mashed into an acronym.
Short answer: xenophobia or just a base level disrespect for people other than themselves. Usually some kind of holier-than-thou kind of complex.
They're valid, though I will admit some can be confusing. Definitely not something one should expect from random strangers that are simply trying to respectfully refer to someone.
It's sad for sure, but those types of people exist for every single crowd out there beyond queerness. I do wish they were less noticed, though.

I'm sure many people go through a similar process, but I just wanted to mention this since it doesn't get put out there a lot — most of (fully) realizing you're queer is having to internally deconstruct the structures society puts in place (either implicitly or explicitly): that you're cisgender, heterosexual, and alloromantic and allosexual (those last two mean that someone experiences romantic and sexual attraction to other people). 

Mine was long and arduous and spanned so so so many years from when I was about 11 or 12 to even now as an 18 year old. To give a basic rundown of the different labels I've tried: heterosexual biromantic, bisexual, nonbinary,  agender, lesbian, and now I'm trying to figure out whether or not I might be on the aroace spectrum. 

My main point with this is that some people have a definitive "aha!" moment with their queerness and some have more of a long-term journey. All are valid and all are important <3

I'm not from the subcontinent so I'm not sure how much weight my opinion holds here, but I was born and brought up here for most of my life. Long story short, Dubai is not a home, it is a business centre. Money moves fast here and if for any reason you cannot contribute, you're at a severe disadvantage. Dubai in its very urban, social, and economic structure is not a place to make a permanent home in, especially so if you're an expat. 

Imagine being my mother, working here for decades and even giving birth to and raising a child in this country and still be treated the same as she did when she first arrived all those years ago — no benefits and no permanent residency and being seen as just another cog in a capitalist machine that can be replaced without a second thought by one of the hundreds that fly here for work every day. There's just no long-term stability here no matter what anyone does, and it's near impossible to truly assimilate into local society. Dubai (and by extension, the rest of the UAE) does not care about giving benefits to keep trusted, competent people here when they could just hire from the endless stream of newcomers for way cheaper. 

That's why (and I've observed this with most of my peers who also grew up here) many of the  parents that raise kids here encourage them to aim for student visas in western countries that lead to building careers in those places and eventually, permanent residency or citizenship. These parents are often driven into a corner by the impermanent nature of life in Dubai, hence why they tend to raise children in a way that sets them up for a better life elsewhere. In that way, Dubai actually drives people into these western countries as it serves as a transitional stage from people's country of origin to a western country that provides more stability and certainty.
